newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Telecoms chiefs say gimmicks threaten advances.
newsitem.headline: Telecoms chiefs say gimmicks threaten advances.

text.p: Advances in telecommunications technology risk being squandered on gimmicks instead of improving the lives of disadvantaged people around the world, industry executives said on Wednesday.

"We seem to be approaching a principal economic goal of many governments around the world with the arrival of universal telephony and sustainable economic growth," said G.B Helman, an executive with Mobile Communication Holdings Inc.

"The increasing use of telecommunications in a universal manner around the world will have profound economic, social and political consequences," Helman told delegates at the Asia Telecoms 97 trade fair.
"But we will not succeed if all we are going to do is give some one a fancier hand-held telephone," he said.
Richard Barber, executive director of the Pacific Telecommunication Council in Hawaii also urged that the amazing new technologies be put to use in areas which risk being left behind.
"Technology provides us with a rich array of possibilities. We must embrace them," he said.
"We need to create centres in remote areas for satellite communications, for information, training and education exchange."

Helman said providing broad-based services, including education and fully interactive forums to facilitate the faster exchange of ideas and technology, would be vital to components of an advanced communications network in the information age.

Barber called on on the world's telecommunications industry leaders to form a new alliance called "Telecorps", modelled on the U.S. Peace Corps which sends young graduates to poorer countries to help in development projects.
Telecorps would be aimed at educating Asia's young people and women in rural areas to help them lead productive lives in some of the most remote parts of the world, Barber said.
"Some new ideas are needed to discuss this great technology we have and how to put it into the hands of the people," he told delegates.

The Internet could hold the key to bridging the information gap, but its guiding purpose was being overshadowed by technical considerations, said Barry Green, senior consultant at Cisco (USA) Pte Ltd.

"There is a lot of talk about phone line capacity, satellite communications, bandwidth and infrastructure. While these are important components to enable communication, the key aspect of what makes the Internet work is people," Green said.
"People are the core of the network and empowering other people through the exchange of information is what the Internet is about," he said.

Heather Hudson, professor of telecommunications management the University of San Francsco said changing the focus of telecommunications from simple economic growth to more broad-based socio-economic development was vital.
"Growth will come as a consequence of improving communications. Development implies the use of telecommunications technology to achieve a range of social as well as economic goals," she said.
